world_behind.title: Dated to a death
world_behind.text: Uzziah reigned in Judah for decades and died a leper, and Isaiah dates his vision to that year rather than to a regnal number. A throne had just been vacated in Jerusalem, and the first thing the prophet reports seeing is an occupied one.

world_behind.title: Inside the temple
world_behind.text: The train filling the house, the smoke, the altar with tongs beside it, the door posts moving: every furnishing named belongs to a sanctuary. Whether Isaiah was physically in the temple or shown it, the vision uses the building his hearers knew, which makes the coal in verse 6 an object anyone could picture.

world_behind.title: A vision the record could have paraphrased
world_behind.text: Nephi had summarized visions before, his father's included, in a few verses. Here he transcribes one whole, in its original first person, with the prophet's confession and cleansing left in. What his colony received was Isaiah's own account of his call. The difference is between hearing that a man was sent and hearing him say yes.

world_behind.title: The credential Nephi claimed
world_behind.text: Two chapters before the block began, Nephi argued that Isaiah could be trusted because "he verily saw my Redeemer, even as I have seen him" (2 Ne. 11:2). This chapter is the report of that seeing. Nephi's case for copying thirteen chapters rests on a vision his readers meet here for the first time.

world_behind.title: A commission nobody would want
world_behind.text: The message Isaiah is given is that his preaching will not work. He is not sent to persuade, and the chapter is honest about it before he has said a word publicly. Prophets in this record are usually shown being rejected; this one is told in advance that rejection is the assignment.

world_behind.title: The stump
world_behind.text: The last verse promises a tenth that returns and is eaten again, and then compares it to a felled tree whose stock remains. Judean hillsides were full of cut oaks and terebinths that regrew from the root. The image is not a promise of rescue from the axe. It is a promise that something survives it.

words.text: The trailing part of a robe, the length of cloth that follows a king into a room. One garment's hem fills the entire temple, which tells a reader the scale of the figure without describing him at all. Isaiah reports what he could take in, and what he could take in was fabric.

The name means burning ones. The record uses the Hebrew plural where the King James adds an English -s, and the creatures are named this way only in this chapter, here and in the Bible alike. They are described entirely by function: six wings, two for the face, two for the feet, two for flying. Four of the six are for covering, so the beings closest to the throne are the most carefully shielded from it.

Two, in the old form the King James Bible keeps for pairs. The record uses the word ten times and the King James Bible seventeen. Here it counts wings, three times in one verse: with twain the seraph covers its face, with twain its feet, with twain it flies. Four of the six wings are spent on concealment and two on motion, and the verse hands over the arithmetic without a word of comment.

"Make the heart of this people fat" (v. 10): fat here means dull, padded, unable to feel what touches it. A modern reader brings a different sense. The word surfaces twice more in this Isaiah block and both times it means well fed: the waste places of the fat ones (2 Ne. 15:17), and leanness sent among his fat ones (2 Ne. 20:16). Prosperity and insensibility share the one word, and this verse takes the second sense.

cites.quote: Make the heart of this people fat

spans.text: Make the heart of this people fat

words.text: The older sense is laid waste, emptied out, rather than squandered. The one other place this record uses the word runs the modern way, sheaves gathered into garners so that they are not wasted (Alma 26:5), and the two senses are easy to tell apart: grain is wasted by being spilled, a city is wasted by having nobody left in it. Isaiah says the second three times over in one breath, "without inhabitant" (v. 11), without man, utterly desolate.

An older English name for the terebinth, a large tree of the Judean hills that grows again from the stump after felling. It is paired with the oak, which does the same. Isaiah ends a chapter of desolation on a piece of ordinary forestry, and the record keeps the archaic name.

phrases.term: Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of Hosts
phrases.text: The only attribute repeated three times anywhere in scripture, and the two creatures call it out to each other. John hears the same words from the living creatures around the throne in his own vision, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty" (Rev. 4:8). The second half of the verse then does the opposite of confining that holiness to the temple: the whole earth is full of his glory.

phrases.term: Wo is unto me! for I am undone
phrases.text: Isaiah's first words in his own book are a self-sentence. He has just finished pronouncing six woes on other people in the previous chapter, and the seventh lands on him. The verb is the older one: undone means ruined, come apart, the way a seam is undone, so the crisis he reports is in his condition. A prophet discovers he belongs on his own list before he is sent to read it out.

phrases.term: Having a live coal in his hand
phrases.text: The remedy is taken from the altar, from the place of sacrifice, and it is applied to the exact part of him he had just named as unclean. Nothing is said about how the seraph carries fire, though the tongs are mentioned for the coal's removal from the altar. The cleansing is specific, physical, and painful-looking, and Isaiah does not describe it hurting.

The volunteering happens after the cleansing and before the assignment is disclosed. Isaiah does not ask what the message is. The same three-word answer appears in Abraham's account of a council where one volunteers and is chosen, so the record's readers meet the formula twice, and both times it is spoken by someone who has already been prepared.

The chapter's most consequential variant, and it changes the commission. In the King James text Isaiah is told to say "Hear ye indeed, but understand not" (Isa. 6:9), an imperative that reads as a command to the people to fail. Here the second clause is past tense and third person: they heard, and they did not understand. What was a sentence pronounced on them becomes a report of what already happened, and the prophet is describing his audience rather than cursing it.

phrases.term: And be converted and be healed
phrases.text: The King James has the people "convert" (Isa. 6:10) as something they do. This reading makes it passive, something done to them, and pairs it with healing in the same construction. Read with the variant in verse 9, the pair points the same direction: hearing and turning are things that happen to a person who is willing.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: The interjection is respelled, as it was two chapters ago
verses.text: Woe becomes wo, and unto is added. The same single-letter substitution runs through every occurrence in 2 Nephi 15, so the practice is not local to one verse; it is how this text spells the word wherever it falls.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: The pronoun changes position in the answer
verses.text: Isaiah's "Then said I" is reordered here, and the effect is to put the speaker before the speech rather than after it. Nothing is added to the sentence and nothing is taken away. Only the order moves, in the verse where the prophet volunteers.

verses.label: v. 9–10
verses.title: Two commands become a report of what already happened
verses.text: This is the largest change in the chapter and it is grammatical. In Isaiah the prophet is told to say "hear ye indeed, but understand not," an instruction in the imperative. Here the verbs move into the past tense and the third person, so the clause describes what the people did rather than commanding what they must do. Verse 10 makes a matching shift, turning an active verb passive.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: A verb of reply becomes a verb of speech
verses.text: Isaiah has "Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered." Here answered becomes said. The record loses the sense that the second speaker is responding to the first, in a verse where the question is "how long" and the reply is a sentence of desolation.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: The last variants shift a reason and a location
verses.text: Verse 12's and becomes for, converting a sequence into a cause. Verse 13 replaces "in it" with there and a singular it with they. The variants close with three small substitutions, in a chapter whose one large change was the grammar of the commission.

chapter.title: A call story placed after the woes
chapter.text: Isaiah's commission is chronologically the beginning of his ministry, and the book puts it in chapter 6, after the vineyard and the six woes. A reader meets the message first and the messenger's credentials second. Nephi used the same order: he quoted Isaiah for four chapters before showing where the authority came from.

chapter.title: Cleansing precedes sending, and both precede understanding
chapter.text: Five steps stand in five verses and none is out of order. Verse 5 is the seeing and the undoing, "Wo is unto me! for I am undone." Verses 6 and 7 are the cleansing, done by someone else with an instrument, "a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar," and the verdict, "thine iniquity is taken away." Verse 8 is the volunteering, "Here am I; send me." Verse 9 is the assignment. Nothing between the confession and the commission is performed by the man who receives it.

chapter.title: The variants soften a command into a diagnosis
chapter.text: Verses 9 and 10 are among the harshest lines in scripture in their King James form, and both are quoted in that form by later writers. This reading turns the first into a report of what the people did and makes conversion something received. The change does not make the chapter comfortable; it changes who is responsible for the deafness.

chapter.title: This is the vision Nephi's argument depends on
chapter.text: Having claimed that Isaiah saw the Redeemer as he and Jacob had, Nephi copies the report of the seeing. His father's own first vision had opened the same way, with God "sitting upon his throne" (1 Ne. 1:8) among numberless angels, so the record's founding vision and the prophet's founding vision share their first image. That is not argued in the text; it is simply available to a reader moving through the plates in order.

chapter.title: Holiness is the chapter's whole subject
chapter.text: The threefold cry, the covered faces, the unclean lips, the coal from the altar, the holy seed at the end: every movement is about the distance between what is holy and what is not, and about the one procedure that closes it. Nothing in the chapter is about behavior in the ordinary sense.

chapter.title: The end is a stump
chapter.text: The question at verse 11 is two words, "how long," and the answer runs to the end of the chapter without a date: "until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate." Verse 13 offers the only consolation and immediately damages it, "there shall be a tenth, and they shall return, and shall be eaten." What survives that is a stump, "whose substance is in them when they cast their leaves." The remnant figure the record uses at 1 Nephi 10:12–14, 2 Nephi 3:5, and Jacob 5 is set here, in its least sentimental form.

applications.title: Date your own vision to a loss
applications.text: Isaiah fixes his experience of God to the year a king died. Identify the season when something you counted on ended, and ask what you learned about who was actually on the throne. The pairing is often clearer in retrospect than at the time.

applications.title: Say the undone sentence
applications.text: Before asking for anything, try naming your condition rather than your failures: the honest state you are in. Isaiah's confession is one clause long and does not itemize, and the coal comes after it.

applications.title: Let the coal touch the actual fault
applications.text: The cleansing landed on the mouth because the mouth was named. Identify the specific thing you have been asking God to work around, and ask him instead to address that, in those words.

applications.title: Volunteer before you hear the terms
applications.text: Once this week, say yes to something for God's purposes without first establishing what it will require. Isaiah's answer came before the assignment, and the assignment was worse than he could have guessed.

applications.title: Preach without requiring results
applications.text: Whatever you have been asked to teach, serve, or say, do it once this month with the outcome explicitly released. The prophet in this chapter was told his work would not land, and he went anyway, for sixty years.

applications.title: Look for the stump
applications.text: When something in your life has been cut down, resist both denial and despair long enough to check for the stock. Isaiah's last word about a devastated nation is that the root is holy seed, and roots are not visible from above.

questions.text: What throne in my life has recently emptied, and what did I reach for first?
When did I last encounter God's holiness in a way that changed how I spoke the next day?
If I finished the sentence "I am undone because...", what would the honest ending be?
What would I be free to volunteer for if I actually believed my sin was purged?
Where have I been hearing indeed and not understanding, and what would it take to be converted?
What am I currently asking "how long" about, and can I live with an answer like the one Isaiah got?
